opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and I think it's one where the field has shifted quite a bit over the last few years.

When we started working on locomotion with reinforcement learning, the "task" was actually pretty broad in one sense and very narrow in another. Broad because we weren't telling the robot *how* to walk. We weren't specifying foot placements or gait patterns. We just said, "follow this velocity command, don't fall, don't waste too much energy." But it was narrow because the robot was only ever doing that one thing. It was a walking policy, and that's all it was.

So I tend to think of specificity along a couple of axes. One is how much you constrain the *behavior*: are you prescribing the motion, or just the outcome? The other is how much you constrain the *scope*: is this one skill, or a family of skills, or something open-ended?

With RL in simulation, I've found you usually want to be as unspecific as possible about the behavior. You define the objective and let the optimization find the solution, because it often finds things you wouldn't have designed by hand. But in practice you end up adding reward terms to shape it, to keep it smooth, to make it transfer to the real hardware. So there's always this tension. The more you specify, the more predictable and deployable it is, but the more you're baking in your own assumptions.

Where it gets really interesting now is when you go to things like loco-manipulation, or general-purpose humanoids, where the task isn't "walk forward at one meter per second" but something like "go open that door" or "pick up that box." Then the definition of the task itself becomes fuzzy. You can't easily write a reward for every possible thing a person might ask. That's where people are starting to combine learned low-level controllers, which are quite specific and robust, with higher-level models that interpret much less specific instructions, maybe from language or from demonstrations.

So my general view is that the low level should be very well defined, very robust, almost like a reliable API for the body, and then the specificity can loosen as you go up the hierarchy. Getting that interface right, deciding what the high level commands and what the low level is responsible for, is honestly one of the hardest design decisions in the whole system.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's actually something I think about a lot, because when we say "task" in legged robotics, that word is doing a lot of hidden work. There's a huge range of specificity, and where you sit on that range changes almost everything about how you train and what you get out.

At one end, you have something extremely specific: walk forward at one meter per second on flat ground. That's easy to define, easy to reward, and the robot will do exactly that, and nothing else. At the other end, you have something like "get from point A to point B in this building," where the task is defined by an outcome, and the robot has to figure out whether that means walking, climbing stairs, stepping over a gap, maybe getting up after it falls. For me, the interesting space is in the middle, and the question I usually ask is: what's the minimal thing I actually need to specify for the behavior I want to emerge?

The reason that matters is that every detail you add to the task definition is a constraint on the solution. If I tell the robot the exact gait, the exact foot placement, I'm baking in my prior about how a legged robot should move, and my prior is often wrong, or at least suboptimal for that particular hardware. We saw this very clearly on ANYmal. When we loosened the task to just "track this velocity command and don't fall," and let the policy discover how, it came up with behaviors we wouldn't have designed by hand, and they were more robust. So underspecifying, in a sense, is a feature.

But there's a limit. If you underspecify too much, you get two failure modes. One is reward hacking, where the robot finds some degenerate strategy that technically satisfies your objective, like vibrating in place or dragging a limb. The other is just that the learning problem becomes too hard, because the reward is too sparse or too ambiguous and the policy never gets off the ground, literally. So in practice, I'd say the task definition ends up being an iterative conversation between you and the robot. You state the outcome you care about, you watch what it does, and then you add just enough shaping, through rewards, through curriculum, through how you design the terrains, to rule out the behaviors you don't want without dictating the ones you do.

The other dimension I'd add is that the right level of specificity depends on what the policy is for. If it's a low-level locomotion controller that a higher-level planner or a human is going to command, then "track velocity" is the right abstraction, because it exposes a clean interface. If you're training something end-to-end for a whole mission, the task has to be defined in terms of the environment and the goal, and the locomotion becomes an implicit subproblem. Both are valid, but they're very different objects, and I think a lot of confusion in the field comes from comparing results across those levels as if they were the same thing.

astra-6.text:
I think there are different levels at which you can define a task. For locomotion, for example, we usually specify a desired velocity: move forward at this speed, or turn at this rate. We don’t specify where every foot should go or how each joint should move. That’s something the policy figures out.

But that’s already a fairly narrow task. At a higher level, you might say, “Go to the kitchen,” and then something needs to translate that into commands the locomotion policy can execute. So the specificity really depends on where you draw the boundary between what you tell the robot and what you expect it to figure out for itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what level you’re looking at. You could describe a task as “go to the kitchen and bring me a glass of water,” but that contains a lot of smaller tasks. The robot has to navigate, identify the glass, grasp it, and so on. And even something like walking can be specified at different levels: do you tell the robot where to put every foot, or do you just give it a desired velocity and let it figure out the motion?

In our work on locomotion, we typically use that second kind of specification. We tell the robot how we want it to move, and we train a policy to produce the joint actions that accomplish that. So the task is quite simple to express, but the behavior required to solve it can be very complex.
